previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, prior stents, diabetes, and diastolic heart failure was admitted for shortness of breath, fatigue, and pleuritic chest pain. Initial evaluation revealed an elevated D-dimer, and a CT pulmonary angiogram confirmed bilateral pulmonary emboli. A lower extremity ultrasound showed an acute deep vein thrombosis in the left common femoral vein. Troponins and BNP were normal, and EKG showed no acute changes. He was started on heparin and transitioned to warfarin with Lovenox bridging. The patient remained stable on room air, with persistent mild dyspnea on exertion leading to a two-night stay. He was discharged home on anticoagulation with instructions for INR monitoring and further evaluation for an unprovoked thrombotic event.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ yo M with hx of CAD, HTN, DM and recent admission for DVT/PE 
who presented with bilateral lower extremity pain.  
 
#. Lower extremity pain: Patient presented with bilateral lower 
extremity pain right worse then left. PMH notable for CAD and 
recent admission for DVT/PE.  Etiology of lower extremity pain 
was unclear. Exam was notable for mild tenderness over the top 
of the R foot and mild bilateral calf tenderness without 
erythema, swelling, decreased pulses, palor or changes in motor 
function and strength.  Differential included peripheral 
neuropathy, radicular pain, arthritis, gout, compartment 
syndrome, clot. Bilateral lower extremity ultrasound did showed 
improved clot burden on warfarin.  There was concern for 
avascular necrosis of the navicular bone on the right, however 
x-ray did not show evidence of this. Bilateral ankle pain could 
be arthritis however no evidence of inflammation. There were no 
metabolic abnormalities to account for cramping.  ESR was within 
normal limits making an inflammatory or autoimmune process 
unlikely.  Patient was given standing Tylenol and discharged 
with small supply of PRN Percocet.  Patient was seen by physical 
therapy who felt he was able to ambulate and could safely go 
home. He should follow up with podiatry on discharge.Metabolic 
blood values ok so don't explain cramps. Unlikely rheum related, 
but presentation unusual  

Chronic Issues 
# DVT/PE - Clot burden improved on warfarin, patient continued 
on warfarin.
# CAD - Stable, continued on home aspirin, statin, beta blocker 
and Plavix.
# HTN - Normotensive. Continued on home beta- blocker, 
diltiazem, and valsartan.
# dCHF- On Lasix as needed for lower extremity edema. No edema 
on admission. 
# DM - Poorly controlled. Discharged on home regimen.
# Hypothyroid- Continued on home levothyroxine.
# GERD- Put on home omeprazole instead of nexium while in house.

- Hold Coumadin on day of discharge, restart on day after

- Follow up with podiatry

femoral and femoral veins.  There has been clearing of thrombus from the
confluence of the greater saphenous vein with the common femoral vein on the
prior study.
